segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Social Dialogue

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hi, Mei. Have you got a minute? I wanted to ask about the data project you mentioned last week.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Sure, come in. I was just looking at the numbers now, actually.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Great. So, the council asked us to compare the two recycling schemes, right?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's right. The old scheme and the new one. But I have to warn you, the data isn't as clean as I'd hoped.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, the old scheme ran for eighteen months, but the new one has only been running for six. So we're not really comparing like with like.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I see. So the time periods are different.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Exactly. And there's another problem. The old scheme covered three neighbourhoods, but the new one covers five.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So the new one has more households.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes, about 40 per cent more. Which means the total amount recycled will naturally be higher, even if each household recycles less.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Right. So we should compare rates per household, not totals.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's what I think. But my manager wants a simple total figure for the report.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hmm. Could you give both? A total and a rate?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I could, but it might confuse the readers. They'll just look at the biggest number.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: True. But if you explain it clearly, maybe it's better than hiding the problem.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You're probably right. Actually, let me show you something. Look at this chart.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Okay. The blue line is the old scheme?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: No, the blue line is the new scheme. The orange line is the old one. Sorry, I should have labelled them more clearly.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: No problem. So the blue line starts higher, but then it drops.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yes. In the first two months, the new scheme recycled more per household. But by month five, it was actually lower than the old scheme.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That's interesting. Why do you think that happened?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I'm not sure yet. It could be that people were excited at first, and then lost interest. Or it could be that the new bins are harder to use.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Have you asked the residents?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Not yet. That's actually what I wanted to ask you about. Do you think we should run a short survey?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Definitely. Even a small survey would help explain the numbers. Maybe twenty or thirty households?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That's what I was thinking. I'll draft some questions this afternoon.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Good. And when you write the report, make sure you say clearly that the two schemes ran for different lengths of time.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I will. Thanks for the advice.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Any time. Let me know how the survey goes.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Social Monologue

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Hello, everyone. This is a short announcement about the community data workshop taking place next Saturday. The workshop is aimed at residents who want to understand the statistics that appear in local news and council reports. You do not need any previous experience, and you do not need to bring a laptop. We will provide everything you need.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The workshop will run from ten in the morning until three in the afternoon, with a break for lunch. Lunch is not provided, but there is a café on the ground floor of the building. The workshop is free, but places are limited to twenty people, so please register in advance. You can register by calling the library or by sending an email to the address on the poster.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: During the morning, we will look at three common mistakes that people make when reading statistics. The first is confusing correlation with causation. Just because two things happen at the same time does not mean that one causes the other. The second is ignoring the size of the group being studied. A survey of ten people is not as reliable as a survey of a thousand. The third is accepting an average without asking what kind of average it is. As you may know, the mean and the median can be very different.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: In the afternoon, we will work in small groups. Each group will receive a short article containing some statistics, and your task will be to identify any misleading claims. At the end of the day, each group will present its findings to the others. This is not a test, and there are no right or wrong answers. The aim is simply to practise asking good questions.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, I should mention that the workshop will be repeated next month, on a weekday evening, for people who cannot attend on Saturday. If you would like to come to the evening session instead, please tell us when you register. And if you have any questions, you can ask me now or send an email later. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Academic Discussion

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good morning, both of you. Thanks for coming. I'd like to discuss your progress on the data analysis module. Let's start with you, Anna. How did you find the exercise on averages?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: It was harder than I expected, actually. I thought I understood averages, but then I got confused by the difference between the mean and the median.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's very common. Can you explain the difference now?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: I think so. The mean is the total divided by the number of items. The median is the middle value when the items are arranged in order.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Exactly. And when would you use the median rather than the mean?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: When there are extreme values. Like, if one person earns a lot more than everyone else, the mean goes up, but the median stays the same.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Now, Ben, what about you? How did you find the exercise?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: I found the averages exercise quite straightforward, but I struggled with the section on percentages.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: What was difficult about it?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: I kept mixing up 'per cent' and 'percentage points'. For example, if something goes from 20 per cent to 25 per cent, is that a 5 per cent increase or a 25 per cent increase?

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's a classic trap. What's the answer?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Well, it's an increase of five percentage points, but it's also a 25 per cent increase relative to the original figure.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Correct. And which one should you use in a report?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: It depends on what you want to emphasise. But you should always say which one you're using.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Exactly. Now, Anna, you mentioned that you found the exercise harder than expected. Did you use any particular strategy?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: I tried to draw a small table for each question. That helped me see the numbers more clearly.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: That's a good approach. Ben, did you try anything similar?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Not really. I just read the questions and tried to calculate in my head. Maybe that's why I made mistakes.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: It's possible. Mental calculation is useful, but writing things down reduces errors. I'd suggest trying Anna's method next time.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: I will.

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Good. Now, let's talk about the next assignment. You'll need to compare two datasets and write a short report. The key thing is to be clear about what you're comparing. Don't just say 'the numbers went up'. Say what went up, by how much, and over what period.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Will we need to use graphs?

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Yes, at least one graph. But remember, a graph should make the comparison clearer, not more confusing. Label your axes carefully.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: When is the deadline?

segments.speaker: Tutor
segments.text: Two weeks from Friday. And please submit it electronically. Any questions?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: No, I think that's clear.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Me neither. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: Academic Lecture

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about re-testing, and why it is one of the most powerful tools in education. Many students believe that testing is simply a way of measuring what they have learned. But a large body of research suggests that testing is also a way of producing learning. This is sometimes called the testing effect.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Let me explain what I mean. Suppose you are preparing for an examination. You could read your notes several times. Or you could read them once and then test yourself. Most people believe that re-reading is more effective, because it feels easier. But in controlled experiments, the people who test themselves typically remember more, even though they spend less time studying. The reason is that retrieving information from memory strengthens the memory itself. Re-reading, by contrast, creates a feeling of familiarity without necessarily improving recall.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: However, not all tests are equally effective. The timing matters. If you test yourself immediately after learning something, the test is easy, and the benefit is small. If you wait a day or two, the test becomes harder, but the benefit is greater. This is why spaced testing is more effective than cramming. The same principle applies to the difficulty of the test. If the test is too easy, it produces little benefit. If it is too difficult, you may become discouraged. The ideal is what researchers call desirable difficulty: a test that requires effort but is still achievable.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: There is also a diagnostic benefit. A test taken early in a course can show you what you have misunderstood, so that you can focus your study on the right areas. In this sense, testing is not only a way of measuring learning; it is a way of directing it.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Of course, there are limits. Frequent high-stakes testing can increase anxiety, especially for students who lack confidence. The research therefore supports regular, low-stakes testing rather than constant formal examinations. The goal is not to test more, but to test better.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: For those of you preparing for language examinations, I would suggest a simple experiment. Take a vocabulary list you are currently studying. Instead of reading it repeatedly, cover the meanings and try to recall them. Then check your answers. You may find the process uncomfortable, but that discomfort is often a sign that learning is taking place. Try it for two weeks and compare your results with your usual method. You may be surprised by the difference.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, let me turn to the second part of the lecture, which concerns the role of feedback. Feedback is most effective when it is specific and timely. Telling a student that they are 'wrong' is less useful than explaining why their answer is wrong and how it could be improved. This is why good teachers do not simply mark answers as correct or incorrect; they explain the reasoning. The same principle applies when you are testing yourself: after checking your answers, spend a moment thinking about why you made a mistake. That reflection is where much of the learning happens.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: To summarise, re-testing is effective because it strengthens memory, it reveals gaps in understanding, and it directs future study. But it works best when it is spaced out, appropriately difficult, and followed by specific feedback. Thank you. I'll take questions at the end.
